title: Extreme Heatwave Early Warning and Human Thermal Stress Index
department: National Centre for Medium Range Weather Forecasting (NCMRWF)
description:
In recent years, the frequency, duration, and intensity of heatwaves across India have escalated sharply due to climate change. However, traditional meteorological warnings rely almost exclusively on ambient dry-bulb temperature thresholds. This creates a critical vulnerability:standard forecasts ignore the deadly compounding effects of relative humidity, wind speed, and solar radiation on the human body.
A temperature of 40°C at 20% humidity feels vastly different from 40°C at 70% humidity-the latter can be fatal. Current public health infrastructure lacks localized, impact-based forecasting that translates raw weather data into actual physiological risk, human thermal stress levels, and projected mortality rates.
The challenge is to design an intelligent, localized early warning system that shifts heatwave forecasting from 'what the weather will be' to 'what the weather will do' to human health.
Participants need to build a predictive platform that computes a comprehensive Human Thermal Stress Index (integrating temperature, humidity, wind, and radiation) and links it directly to an automated Mortality Risk Index. The system should offer high-resolution forecasts to help municipal corporations, healthcare systems, and disaster management authorities deploy targeted,preemptive interventions.
Develop algorithms to calculate advanced heat stress metrics such as the Wet-Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT), Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI), or Heat Index (HI) rather than relying on temperature alone. Integrate historical public health, demographic (e.g., elderly or outdoor worker density), and localized weather data to predict heat-induced mortality and hospitalization spikes 3 to 5 days in advance. A dynamic GIS-mapped dashboard providing colorcoded, hyper-local alerts (Zone/Ward level) paired with actionable, automated public health advisories. An API capable of pushing automated SMS/WhatsApp regional alerts or localized triggers for city administration to initiate heat action plans (e.g., opening cooling centers, adjusting power grids, shifting outdoor work hours).
summary: Innovation (4/5): draws on predictive, gis applied to a disaster management problem, placing it in the breakthrough band. Feasibility (3/5): as a software build with moderate integration complexity, a full build is tight for 36 hours and will need scope-cutting. Impact (5/5): reaches a broad public/citizen base within Disaster Management. Tech Depth (5/5): centers on api, gis, infrastructure. Sustainability (4/5): has a clear long-term maintenance path. Scalability (3/5): currently scoped narrowly and would need rework to scale. Total 24/30 -> Green verdict.

detail.title: Extreme Heatwave Early Warning and Human Thermal Stress Index

overview.in_plain_terms: Build a heatwave warning system that predicts what the heat actually does to the human body, not just the raw temperature, combining humidity, wind, and radiation into a real thermal stress and mortality risk index that municipal officials can act on.
overview.why_it_matters: 40°C at 20% humidity and 40°C at 70% humidity are very different threats to human survival, but standard warnings treat them the same. This system finally captures that difference where it matters most, in preventing deaths.
pain_points: Standard heatwave warnings rely almost exclusively on dry-bulb temperature, ignoring humidity, wind, and radiation.
No localized system currently translates raw weather into actual physiological risk and mortality projection.
Public health infrastructure lacks impact-based (versus purely meteorological) heatwave forecasting.
overview.background: Heatwave frequency and severity in India are increasing, but traditional warnings ignore the compounding physiological effects of humidity, wind, and radiation, missing the actual human health risk that temperature alone doesn't capture.
overview.whats_being_asked: A predictive platform computing a Human Thermal Stress Index (integrating temperature, humidity, wind, radiation) linked to an automated Mortality Risk Index, with high-resolution, localized forecasts for municipal use.
expected_solution: Human Thermal Stress Index computation integrating multiple physiological-relevant weather variables.
Automated Mortality Risk Index derived from thermal stress levels.
High-resolution, localized forecasting for municipal decision support.
Impact-based framing shifting from 'what weather will be' to 'what weather will do' to health.

analysis.innovation_scope_note: Moderate-High. Thermal comfort/heat stress indices are an established meteorological-health concept (Heat Index, WBGT, etc.), the innovation is in the mortality-risk linkage and localized, impact-based framing specifically.
analysis.invention_effort_note: High. Requires combining established thermal physiology models with real mortality data correlation, genuine cross-domain (meteorology plus public health epidemiology) technical depth.

competitive_landscape.note: Heat-health warning systems exist as a category, but genuine mortality-risk linkage with localized precision is a more specialized, differentiated approach.

innovation.note: The mortality-risk linkage specifically, connecting thermal stress directly to projected health outcomes, is a genuine, impactful differentiator beyond standard heat indices.

invention.note: Combining thermal physiology modeling with mortality-risk correlation requires genuine cross-domain technical and epidemiological depth.

technical_feasibility.note: Established thermal stress index formulas exist and are usable directly; genuine, validated mortality-risk correlation needs real historical health outcome data, which is harder to access and ethically sensitive to model.

impact_and_benefits.note: Directly addresses preventable heat-related deaths, an unusually severe and compelling impact case.

architecture.note: A thermal-index calculation layer plus a mortality-risk correlation layer, well-understood pattern applied to a sensitive domain.

overall_verdict.reasoning: Strong pick, one of the highest-impact PS in this batch. Build the thermal-stress-index calculation using established, well-validated formulas (this part is solid and achievable), and treat the mortality-risk linkage carefully, using established epidemiological relationships from published research rather than fabricating a mortality model from scratch.

evaluator_lens.biggest_strength: Extremely compelling, well-articulated real-world stakes (the 40°C-at-20%-versus-70%-humidity example makes the core insight immediately clear and important).
evaluator_lens.biggest_risk: Fabricating a 'Mortality Risk Index' without grounding in real published epidemiological research linking thermal stress to actual health outcomes would be a serious, potentially harmful overclaim in a domain where wrong guidance has real consequences.
evaluator_lens.validate_before_commit: Ground your Mortality Risk Index explicitly in published epidemiological research linking heat stress indices to real historical mortality data, cite your sources directly, don't present a self-invented risk formula as if it reflects validated health science.

idea_0_4: Use an established, validated thermal stress index formula (Heat Index, WBGT, or similar) as your foundation, don't invent a new one from scratch.
Research published epidemiological literature linking heat stress to real mortality/morbidity outcomes to ground your risk-index approach.
Split: one person on the thermal-index calculation and weather-data integration, one on the mortality-risk research and modeling.
prototype_4_22: Build your Human Thermal Stress Index calculation using established formulas with real local weather data (temperature, humidity, wind, radiation).
Build your Mortality Risk Index, explicitly grounded in cited published research relating stress-index thresholds to real health outcome data.
Start your localized, high-resolution forecast output.
integration_22_30: Connect thermal-stress calculation to mortality-risk estimation and localized forecast output end to end.
Validate your thermal stress calculations against established reference values (test against known formula benchmarks) to confirm correctness.
polish_30_36: Build a clear dashboard showing localized thermal stress levels and associated risk categories.
Rehearse being explicit about your Mortality Risk Index's grounding in published research, citing your sources directly, this is important credibility in a sensitive domain.
Prepare to discuss what real deployment validation (against actual local mortality data) would require.
build_plan.how_to_stand_out: Show your system correctly distinguishing two scenarios with the same raw temperature but different humidity, exactly the PS's core example, producing meaningfully different risk levels, that direct demonstration of the actual insight is the clearest possible proof of value.

strengths: Extremely compelling, clearly-articulated real-world stakes make the impact case immediately obvious.
Established thermal stress index formulas provide a solid, correct technical foundation.
weaknesses: Mortality-risk linkage is a genuinely sensitive claim that needs careful, honest grounding in real published research, not fabrication.
Full localized precision across many municipalities needs real local data that may not be fully available.

roles_needed: Public health/epidemiology research person (critical for the mortality-risk component)
team_fit.ideal_ratio: Don't skip the public-health research role, this is the component where getting it wrong has real ethical and credibility stakes.
team_fit.approach: Research established thermal-stress-mortality epidemiological literature thoroughly before building the risk-index component, this grounding is essential, not optional.

ai_buildability_split.ai_can_build_fast: The thermal stress index calculation using established formulas, and the dashboard/visualization layer.
ai_buildability_split.needs_human_judgment: Grounding the mortality-risk component in real, cited epidemiological research rather than a plausible-sounding but fabricated risk formula, this is a genuine ethical and scientific responsibility.
ai_buildability_split.risk_of_leaning_on_ai_only: An AI-generated 'mortality risk formula' without grounding in real published research could present fabricated health-risk numbers with false authority, a genuinely serious issue in a domain where this could influence real public health decisions if taken at face value.

data_resource_availability.status: Established thermal stress index formulas are well-documented and directly usable; real historical mortality data linked to heat events is more limited and sensitive, published epidemiological research provides the credible grounding path instead.
data_resource_availability.backup_plan: Ground your mortality-risk index explicitly in cited published research relationships (e.g. established heat-index-to-excess-mortality correlations from public health literature) rather than attempting to source and model raw mortality data yourself.

judge_qna.question: Where does your Mortality Risk Index actually come from, is it based on real research or invented?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Cite the specific published epidemiological research your risk-index thresholds and relationships are grounded in, be completely direct if any part is a reasonable approximation versus directly sourced, this is an area demanding real honesty.
judge_qna.follow_up: How would you validate this against actual local historical mortality data if it became available?

judge_qna.question: How does your system handle the humidity-versus-dry-heat distinction that's central to the PS's premise?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Show a direct comparison, two scenarios with identical temperature but different humidity, producing meaningfully different thermal stress and risk outputs, demonstrating you've actually captured the core physiological insight, not just added humidity as a decorative extra input.
judge_qna.follow_up: What's the biggest driver of thermal stress in your model, humidity, wind, or radiation, and does that match established heat-physiology science?
